newsitem.title: FRANCE: Foreign bond buyers come back to France belatedly.
newsitem.headline: Foreign bond buyers come back to France belatedly.

text.p: New figures show foreign investors starting to return to the French bond market after a massive purge of holdings earlier in the year but they may have missed out on chances for big gains, analysts said on Friday.
"The large selloff movement is over...but there won't be a massive return. It's too late," said Morgan Stanley's Eric Chaney. "The bargains have been had," said Nomura's Sonja Gibbs.
Finance ministry data released on Friday showed that non- residents were net buyers of French government bonds in September for the first time since November 1995.
Foreigners bought a net 1.89 billion francs ($362.2 million) of government bonds (OATs) and shorter-dated BTANs in September after selling a net 14.15 billion the previous month.

But net buying for September was still way down on year earlier purchases of 16.96 billion. And figures for the first nine months of 1996 showed net sales of 152.24 billion compared with net purchases of 68.95 billion.

The foreign sell-off was triggered by a transport strike that shut down the country for more than three weeks last December, fears over France's weakening economy and worries it would not hit deficit targets to qualify for monetary union.

But what foreign investors did not reckon on was a wall of cash from domestic insurance companies that supported the market and drove the risk premium on 10-year French bonds over their German counterparts to below parity.
"The common refrain was that the foreigners were pulling out. Well the foreigners did pull out and it didn't go down -- thanks to the domestics," said one trader.

Forecasts last December called for the French 10-year spread over Germany to be 60 to 70 basis points by end 1996. Instead, the spread, which measures the yield difference, now is negative in favour of France. It touched a low of minus 11 on Friday.

The trigger for the wave of domestic portfolio reallocation away from cash and into bonds this year was a cut in the interest rate on a popular tax-free savings vehicle Livret A to 3.5 percent from 4.5 percent, she said.
Partly driving the return of foreign investors now is that so many indexed funds are underweight in France, said Gibbs.

Like Morgan Stanley's Chaney, she does not expect non-residents "to come back in droves. But "there is some perception there could be a little bit more to go in Europan bond markets and France being part of the core, if even only by reason of the political will, stands to benefit," she said.
While France's economy was still bleak with 12.6 percent unemployment, the government's political will to be part of the European single currency eased investor risk, economists said.

President Jacques Chirac on Thursday strongly reiterated France's commitment to monetary union. "Mr. Chirac wants it," said Chaney. "The spectre of a confidence crisis which resulted in high risk premia on French assets has practically vanished."

But Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais said the chief virtue of the French bond market was its defensive quality as it generally outperforms in a falling market, supported by domestic investors who are not about to shift their funds.
